meta.name: Pembroke Welsh Corgi Puppy Checklist
meta.excerpt: Corgi puppy prep has some unique spinal-health items most checklists miss — including ramp setup and exercise limits that matter especially for this breed.
meta.meta_description: Pembroke Welsh Corgi puppy checklist: supplies, first-week plan, spine management from day one, and what the first vet visit should include.

intro.label: Before They Arrive
intro.heading: What to Have Ready Before Your Corgi Puppy Comes Home
intro.html:
Corgis are adaptable, outgoing, and settle into new homes comfortably. The breed-specific prep items that standard puppy checklists miss: ramp setup for any furniture the dog will access, strict food measurement from day one, and an honest plan for managing the herding nipping behavior with children.

Standard priorities apply: insurance before the first vet visit, puppy class enrolled before pickup.

care.label: The Full List
care.heading: Supplies Checklist
care.html:
Containment & Sleep

  • Medium crate with divider — right size for adult Corgi; use divider initially
  • Dog bed — Corgis can be destructive chewers as puppies; a washable mat works for early months
  • Dog ramp — for couch and bed if the dog will have furniture access; starting this habit young prevents cumulative jump-down spinal stress

Feeding

  • Stainless bowls + measuring cup — portion control is non-negotiable; Corgis gain weight easily and obesity severely worsens IVDD risk
  • Small-to-medium breed puppy food — ask the breeder what they've been feeding

Collar, Harness & Leash

  • Flat collar + ID tag
  • Harness + 6-foot leash — harness recommended for leash attachment
  • Long line — for recall training

Grooming

  • Undercoat rake — start from day one for tolerance building
  • Slicker brush
  • Wide-toothed metal comb — for the ruff and behind ears
  • Nail clippers

Toys & Enrichment

  • Kong (medium) — for crate settling and mental stimulation
  • Puzzle feeder — Corgis need mental challenge; puzzle feeding is enrichment and slows eating
  • Tug toy — for structured play

Health & Safety

  • Pet insurance — before first vet visit
  • Puppy class enrolled
  • Vet appointment within 3 days
  • Enzyme cleaner

special.label: First Week
special.heading: First Week Plan and Corgi-Specific Notes
special.html:
Day 1–2: Settling In

Corgis are confident and adapt to new homes quickly. Start crate training from night one. Begin grooming handling with the undercoat rake (with treats) from day one — Corgis that tolerate brushing as puppies are much easier to groom during seasonal shedding as adults. Address the herding instinct (nipping at heels) with immediate redirection every single time it happens.

Day 3: First Vet Visit

Ask your vet to:

  • Review breeder health clearances (OFA hip, PRA DNA test)
  • Discuss spinal health — baseline weight establishment, appropriate exercise limits during growth, when to consider PennHIP if desired
  • Vaccine schedule and prevention protocol

Week 1: Weight and Spine from Day One

Establish the measured feeding routine from the first day. Weigh the puppy at each vet visit and track against breed-appropriate growth charts. Limit jumping on/off furniture from the start — ramps make this easy. Exercise limits: 5 minutes per month of age to protect developing joints and spine.

Most Common Mistake

Free-feeding or overfeeding. Corgis are extraordinarily food-motivated and will eat past satisfaction. An overweight Corgi experiences significantly elevated IVDD risk — the additional load on the already-stressed elongated spine is measurable. Measure every meal from day one and resist the begging. The cuteness of the begging face is real; so are the consequences of giving in consistently.

faq.q: When should I start training my Corgi puppy?
faq.a: From day one for basic handling, name recognition, and the herding nipping redirection. Formal class by weeks 8–10. Corgis are intelligent and learn quickly with positive reinforcement. Early training establishes the herding behavior management that makes daily life much more pleasant, especially with children in the household.

faq.q: My Corgi puppy nips at heels and ankles. How do I stop it?
faq.a: Redirect immediately, every time, without exception. Say 'leave it' or 'off,' redirect to an appropriate toy, and reward engagement with the toy. Yelping and stopping movement when nipped also works for some dogs. The key is consistency — every person in the household needs to respond the same way. This behavior reduces significantly with age and training; it rarely disappears completely in a Corgi, but becomes manageable.

faq.q: Do I really need a ramp for my Corgi?
faq.a: Ideally yes, if they'll have furniture access. Each individual jump-down from couch height doesn't cause injury, but cumulative impact over years on an elongated spine adds up. Dogs with IVDD history especially benefit from eliminating furniture jumping. Ramps are inexpensive relative to IVDD treatment and building the habit young is much easier than introducing it later.

faq.q: Are Corgis good with other dogs?
faq.a: Generally yes — they're social dogs that usually get along well with other dogs. The herding instinct may show up as attempting to 'herd' other dogs, which not all dogs appreciate. Early socialization with various dog personalities helps Corgis learn appropriate dog-to-dog interactions. Supervision initially with dogs that don't tolerate herding behavior is sensible.
